item.content:encoded:
It’s time for both sides of this great baseball town to come together.
No, not the fans. We know better than to ask for that.
Rather, we mean the Cubs and White Sox themselves, for — a doff of the cap and a drumroll, please — the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team is here.
Beat writers Vinnie Duber (Cubs) and James Fegan (Sox) joined frequent baseball scribe Jeff Agrest and yours truly in selecting a 17-man team: one player at each position in the field, a designated hitter, four starting pitchers, three relievers — one of them designated as closer — and a manager.
Four ironclad rules guided our process:
1. This is a 2026 honor. Reputation doesn’t matter.
2. If it’s too close to call at certain positions, lean into which players we’d rather write into a playoff lineup.
3. All players must appear at their primary positions. No exceptions!
4. OK, fine, Alex Bregman and Miguel Vargas both need to be in there somehow. Besides, if we journalists followed the rules, how would everybody know to hate us?
Our team:
SP1: Sean Burke, Sox
Leads Chicago starters in ERA, strikeouts, opponent batting average — closest we’ve got to an ace.
SP2: Shota Imanaga, Cubs
Other than the gopher balls — so many gopher balls — lefty has been effective.
SP3: Davis Martin, Sox
Sox were 10-1 over his first 11 starts. Finishing kick has been strong, too. (As for in between, don’t ask.)
SP4: Matthew Boyd, Cubs
Still one guy who — if locked in — can get you to the seventh inning of a playoff game.
C: Carson Kelly, Cubs
Good hitter, even better with men in scoring position. Not an All-Star, but we’ll take him.
1B: Munetaka Murakami, Sox
Hamstring injury derailed spectacular start. Still, top 10 in AL in homers, walks is big-time.
2B: Chase Meidroth, Sox
Sorry, Nico Hoerner, but this was an easy call. Meidroth has simply been the better batsman.
3B: Alex Bregman, Cubs
One of the best second halves in baseball, combined with stellar glove work. Tough call, though.
SS: Dansby Swanson, Cubs
Just too great on “D” — and Colson Montgomery didn’t get on base enough to unseat him.
LF: Tristan Peters, Sox
South Side’s best outfielder — an All-Star, don’t forget — gets bumped over by you-know-who.
CF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
But you knew this already. Not bad, Mr. MVP.
RF: Seiya Suzuki, Cubs
His RISP work wasn’t the best, but you take the offensive totals every time.
DH: Miguel Vargas, Sox
Sox’ MVP — there’s no debate about that — simply has to be in our lineup.
RP: Bryan Hudson, Sox
Quality lefty with multiple impressive scoreless streaks and pinpoint control all second half.
RP: Sean Newcomb, Sox
Lefty hangs on to a spot despite a rough September.
Closer: Grant Taylor, Sox
The best reliever in town and the only sane choice for this role.
Manager: Craig Counsell, Cubs
Potentially winning 90 despite one pitching problem after another is nothing to sneeze at.
DISSENSIONS IN THE RANKS
In the end, we were in unison on all but three positions. Fegan backed Vargas at third base and Will Venable at manager, and I wanted Sam Antonacci in left.
Fegan on Vargas: Bregman and Vargas are statistically even, so let’s get sentimental. Vargas has been the rock of a Sox offense otherwise defined by streaks. He’s the proof of concept of their newfound ability to improve hitters. A universally beloved bilingual glue guy in a loose clubhouse, Vargas is the team MVP who laughs hard and works harder. Without him, Sox leadership is talking “meaningful progress” rather than playoffs.
Greenberg on Antonacci: His defense is more mosh pit than ballet, but throw him off his spot because of it? Come on, man. He’s always on base, hits in the clutch and plays with his rear end on fire. How do you not love a young cat with a perverse desire to stand in front of 96 mph and get drilled by it? These Sox aren’t these Sox without his signature brand of — how to put it? — Antonacciness.
Fegan on Venable: His in-game moves miss the mark at times; inarguable since he readily fesses up without prompting. But with how naturally fans and commentators have shifted to second-guessing every crucial move in a division chase, it might surprise locally how well Venable does in AL manager of the year voting, or how the baseball world still views his team cracking the playoffs as coaching alchemy, or how much his constant tinkering is not unique but actually–gasp!–the Sox adhering to modern trends.
Contributing: James Fegan, Vinnie Duber, Jeff Agrest

When the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season comes to a close, it is extremely likely that Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs will be named the National League Most Valuable Player.
At this point, it seems like a foregone conclusion. The only guy in the National League who had something to say about the award race was Shohei Ohtani, but he's on the Injured List and hasn't pitched since July 3. Crow-Armstrong has been the best overall player in baseball this year and he deserves the award. Plus, with about a week left in the 2026 season, he could add some history to his season. There are six players in big league history with a 40-40 season under their belt (40 homers and 40 stolen bases). With two more steals, Crow-Armstrong will join the group, as shared by Bob Nightengale of USA Today Sports.
What A Season From Pete Crow-Armstrong
"There were only four players in baseball history who hit 40 homers and stole 40 bases in a season before 2023: Jose Canseco, Barry Bonds, Alex Rodriguez and Alfonso Soriano," Nightengale wrote. "Now, since MLB implemented rules limiting pickoffs with bigger bases, it may happen for the third time in four seasons if Pete Crow-Armstrong steals [two] bases in the final week, joining Ronald Acuña Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024)."
If you can etch your name on a list in Major League Baseball history with Jose Canseco, Barry Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, Alfonso Soriano, Ronald Acuña Jr. and Shohei Ohtani, that's something that every player would want. You're talking about a few of the very best players in Major League Baseball history. While Bonds, Canseco and Rodriguez aren't in the Hall of Fame, these are MVPs and legends we're talking about. Soriano was a seven-time All-Star and a four-time Silver Slugger Award winner throughout his career. Acuña and Ohtani are two MVPs who are still among the elite of the elite.
Crow-Armstrong can join this group by just recording two more steals. So far this season, he's slashing .280/.371/.578 with a .949 OPS, 45 homers, 107 RBIs, 38 stolen bases, 30 doubles, eight triples and 118 runs scored.
The 24-year-old also is among the game's best overall defensive players in baseball. We're witnessing a truly special season from the young slugger and some history could be on the way. Now, he just needs two more steals to get his name in the record books.

CINCINNATI -- The Chicago Cubs were somber after they defeated the Cincinnati Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park on Sunday because Chicago was thinking about third baseman Alex Bregman, who was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch.
Bregman was injured in the fourth inning with two outs. With the count, 1-2, Busch checked his swing at a pitch thrown by Reds right-hander Luis Mey. The ball made contact with Busch's bat, however, and then hit Bregman while he was in the on-deck circle. Bregman then ran towards the end of the Cubs' dugout before finally going into the clubhouse to get looked at by the team’s trainer.
Bregman was taken to a nearby hospital for X-rays and a CT scan, but the Cubs have yet to announce the seriousness of Bregman’s injury.
“I don’t know anything more than that,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell told reporters. “He had a cut under his eye. He was bleeding from his nose a little bit. It’s pretty swollen. It was below the eye. I honestly thought it hit him in the nose. I thought he had a broken nose, but I knew it hit him somewhere in the face. It’s just an unfortunate accident. I’m hoping and praying he is all right.
“We have to get good results from the hospital first. [Bregman] got hit in the face, so you are worried about his general well-being first. If we get a good report, we’ll move to the next step. I want to get a good report.”
Bregman is in his first season with the Cubs after signing a five-year, $175 million contract last January. He is having a productive season with the Cubbies, slashing .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs and 89 RBI.
Before Sunday’s game, Bregman spoke to Yardbarker about his first season with the Cubs.
"The first half didn’t start out how I wanted it. (I) kept fighting. (I) trusted the process,” Bregman said. “I felt like myself over the last two months. That’s what I expect from myself. I’ve also been super thrilled to be in a position to continue to play postseason baseball, play meaningful games in October. I’ve been fortunate to do that every year of my career, which I don’t take lightly. I’m happy that we put ourselves in the position, so far, to be in.”
Bregman even had a word to say about teammate Pete Crow-Armstrong. To Bregman, PCA is the National League Most Valuable Player, and he has the stats to back it up.
Entering Tuesday’s action against the Marlins, Crow-Armstrong is leading the Majors with 10.5 wins above replacement (per FanGraphs) and 118 runs scored. He could also become the seventh player in MLB history to reach the 40-40 plateau.
“He has been the best player in the sport. It’s not even close,” Bregman said about PCA.

With one week to go in the regular season, the Cubs' magic number to clinch a postseason berth has dropped to one, and their magic number to get home field in a Wild Card series is now six. This means that the Cubs control their own destiny. Win out — six games — and they will be home a week from Tuesday against either the Padres or Phillies. (Easy? No, but it is possible.)
In the meantime, here's who was hot and not for the Cubs over the past week.
Three up
Pete Crow-Armstrong had a very weird, but productive, week
PCA batted .345/.367/.897 (10-for-29) with two doubles, a triple, four home runs, nine RBI, seven runs scored and two stolen bases. That's a 1.264 OPS for the six games, which might actually be good enough to get him another Player of the Week award.
But here's the thing. He put up those numbers while going 0-for-15 with five strikeouts in three of the six games!
That means that in the other three games, he was 10-for-14 (.714) with all those other peripheral numbers.
That's just crazy. Here's his 3-for-4 day against the Braves last Wednesday [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
I keep saying this but I have to say it one more time: Savor this PCA season, we have not seen anything like it from a Cubs player — or most MLB players! — in most of our lifetimes. I hope he can steal two bases against the Marlins this week so he'd join the 40/40 club at Wrigley Field.
And remember, PCA is only 24. Who knows? He might do this again next year!
David Peterson is getting hot at just the right time
In his two starts over the week ending Sunday, Peterson threw 12 innings, allowed six hits and two runs, walked four and struck out 14. For his last three starts, which include two against postseason teams (Braves and Brewers), Peterson has a 1.65 ERA and 1.163 WHIP and 18 strikeouts in 16.1 innings. (And the run charged to him against Atlanta scored after he left the game.)
I think the Cubs might have to consider Peterson for a Wild Card series start.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Daniel Palencia appears to be back
Palencia pitched just twice over the week, but the second outing was two scoreless innings against the Reds Saturday, the first time he'd thrown two full innings in a game since April 2025. The best news is that in that two-inning outing, Palencia threw eight of his 20 pitches at 100 miles per hour, a level he had trouble hitting in his first few outings back.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
I don't think I have to tell you how much having a productive Palencia would mean for the Cubs in the postseason.
Three down
Nico Hoerner is still struggling
Remember when Nico was hitting at MVP level in April?
He's had a rough time since then. Over the six games he batted just .250/.280/.292 (6-for-24) with one double.
Nico's offensive numbers are down this year and he's only going to post a bit more than 2 bWAR after a 6.2 bWAR season in 2025.
Hopefully he can turn it on in October, and continue playing solid defense at second base.
Clay Holmes got roughed up by the Reds
Holmes has had a couple of clunkers since joining the Cubs — this week against the Reds and the previous week against the Marlins.
The good news is that both of those starts were on the road. In four Wrigley Field starts since joining the Cubs, Holmes has a 1.14 ERA and 1.014 WHIP in 23.2 innings, with 18 strikeouts and only one home run allowed.
He'll likely start Thursday against the Marlins (though currently that game is listed as TBD for the Cubs starter), which would set him up for a start in the Wild Card series the following week. If that series winds up at Wrigley, I'd seriously consider Holmes for one of the starts.
Edward Cabrera had a rough transition to relieving, but maybe there's hope
Cabrera's first relief outing for the Cubs probably went an inning too long, as he was left in for a third inning of work after finishing the seventh and throwing a scoreless eighth against the Braves last Wednesday. Craig Counsell left him out there in a 4-3 game and he served up a two-run homer to Drake Baldwin in the ninth.
Things were better for Cabrera in a scoreless inning against the Reds in a low-leverage situation on Sunday. He allowed a hit and a walk, but got out of the inning with a double play. He threw only nine pitches, two of which hit 99. Perhaps shorter outings would be better for Cabrera.

item.content:encoded:
The Cubs are as close to securing a trip back to the postseason as possible.
The North Siders need just a single win, or a single D-backs loss, over the regular season’s final week to clinch a spot in the NL Wild Card round.
Who will the Cubs play? And where will those games be played? Those questions won’t be answered until next weekend, most likely.
But with just six games remaining until playoff baseball, who will the Cubs need to step up in order to make a run at the World Series in a National League field filled with strong contenders such as the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves?
Here’s a look at who the Cubs need to do their part to get back to the Fall Classic for the first time since 2016:
Who will step up at the back end of the 'pen?
Who will close games? This is by far the Cubs’ biggest, and potentially most important, question that needs to be answered. Will it be Jacob Webb, who leads the team with nine saves, or will former closer Daniel Palencia, who just spun two scoreless innings in one of his most impressive outings of the year, be able to take that role? Manager Craig Counsell, who has used 14 pitchers to record saves this season, will be tasked with piecing together a bullpen that has limited experience in those situations.
The Cubs need Webb, who spun a scoreless outing in 24 straight appearances from June to August, to get back into form after allowing 11 runs over his past 7 2/3 innings (nine games). If Palencia, who has thrown 6 1/3 straight scoreless innings, can also replicate his success from 2025, it could be a major boost for a club that entered Cincinnati converting just four of its past 12 save opportunities.
Deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn and lefty Ryan Rolison could also play a big factor late in games, but there’s also a secret weapon waiting out in the bullpen …
Can Cabrera be a reliable relief option?
That brings us to Edward Cabrera, who returned from a recurring blister injury on his pitching hand on Sept. 15 in a multi-inning relief role. That will be his job going forward as the Cubs hope shorter outings can not only keep him healthy, but potentially provide a small uptick in velocity. Cabrera’s first relief experience had mixed results (two runs in 2 1/3 IP), but he came out of the bullpen Sunday and tossed a scoreless inning on just nine pitches.
The best-case scenario of this temporary move to the bullpen? Cabrera turns into this year’s version of the Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki, which would immediately help stabilize the back end of the Cubs’ bullpen. Cabrera’s season hasn’t gone to plan, posting a 5.68 ERA in 15 starts between three stints on the injured list, but he still has a chance to make a significant impact when it matters most.
PCA still doing MVP things in October
Is it really fair to ask more of Pete Crow-Armstrong? After going yard again Sunday, the Cubs slugger is tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the most home runs in the Major Leagues. He leads Chicago in batting average (.280), homers (45), RBIs (107), stolen bases (38), runs scored (118), on-base percentage (.371), hits (170), triple (eight) and games played (156). Got all that? Simply put, he’s put together one of the most impressive offensive seasons in Cubs history and he’s not done.
But he will need others to contribute in October. While run production starts with Crow-Armstrong, even if he performs to his NL MVP front-runner ability, he can’t do it all himself. The North Siders have to count on Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Ian Happ, Alex Bregman and Michael Busch below him in the lineup to generate scoring chances.
Holmes stepping up as playoff ace
Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd are the clear No. 1 and No. 2 options for the playoffs, but Counsell hasn’t yet revealed who will pitch in the all-important Game 1. Holmes had a strong August (1.55 ERA in five starts) in his return to the big leagues after missing nearly three months with a right fibula fracture, but he’s allowed 16 ER in just 15 1/3 IP across three starts in September (9.39 ERA).
That’s a worrying trend for a club with limited starting options in the postseason, but Shota Imanaga has stabilized recently after a down stretch in August, and veteran Kevin Gausman can provide multiple innings in whatever role the Cubs need during the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.

Pete Crow-Armstrong alcanzó una combinación estadística inédita durante la contundente victoria 9-1 de los Chicago Cubs sobre los Cincinnati Reds. El jardinero terminó la jornada con tres imparables, dos carreras impulsadas, tres anotadas y una base robada.
Crow-Armstrong conectó su cuadrangular número 45 de la temporada e igualó a Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de las Grandes Ligas. También llegó a 30 dobles y 38 bases robadas, convirtiéndose en el primer jardinero central de la historia con al menos 40 jonrones, 30 dobles y 30 robos dentro de una misma campaña.
La actuación confirmó el crecimiento de un jugador capaz de influir en distintas áreas del juego. A su producción de poder agregó velocidad en las bases y una presencia constante en la ofensiva de Chicago, que se mantiene en plena lucha por asegurar su lugar en la postemporada.
Michael Conforto y Seiya Suzuki también conectaron cuadrangulares por los Cubs. Desde el montículo, David Peterson limitó a Cincinnati a una carrera y tres imparables durante seis entradas. La única anotación de los Reds llegó mediante un jonrón de JJ Bleday.
Chicago continúa entre los principales aspirantes a los comodines de la Liga Nacional. Los Cubs comparten la parte alta de esa clasificación con San Diego, mientras Filadelfia se mantiene cerca después de vencer 7-2 a los Mets.

item.content:encoded:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.
Will Schwarber or PCA lead the Majors in home runs?
Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong is putting the finishing touches on a season for the ages - one that may very well go down as the best in the 150-year history of the Chicago Cubs. One last feather in his cap would be achieving a 40/40 season. To do that, he'll need two stolen bases over the next week to join one of baseball's most exclusive clubs.
He's already set a career-high with 38 bags, to go along with 45 home runs, 30 doubles and 107 runs batted in, but the 40/40 club would be the cherry on top. It feels like some context is important, though, because I feel like his bid for history is flying a bit under the radar outside Chicago - and rule changes made during the last MLB CBA talks could be to blame.
As Bob Nightengale of USA Today pointed out in his weekend column, just four players accomplished a 40/40 season prior to 2023: Jose Canseco, Barry Bonds, Alex Rodriguez and Alfonso Soriano. But since then, Ronald Acuna Jr. and Shohei Ohtani have both done it, and PCA could be the third with a strong final week.
Pete Crow-Armstrong on the brink of joining baseball's 40/40 club
That shouldn't take away from the accomplishments of Ohtani, Acuna Jr. or Crow-Armstrong. But we also shouldn't ignore the impact the rule changes have had on the game (which are exactly what the league hoped for when it made them). For context, in 2022, there were 2,486 stolen bases across Major League Baseball. The 2026 regular season isn't even over yet and we're already over 3,000.
PCA pseudo-joined that group of aforementioned stars with a double in the early innings Sunday, becoming just the sixth player in MLB history with 30+ doubles, 35+ stolen bases and 40+ homers in a season (the others being Ohtani, Acuna Jr., Soriano, Rodriguez and Canseco). As he closes in on 40/40 and the first MVP award of his career, rule change or not, Crow-Armstrong has shown his breakout 2025 was no fluke and he's ready to lead the charge into the next era of Chicago Cubs baseball.

The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman shared a graphic selfie Sunday after suffering a frightening facial injury from a foul ball during an MLB game.
Bregman was struck during the fourth inning of Chicago's 9-1 win over the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. Teammate Michael Busch fouled a pitch from Luis Mey, and the ball bounced into Bregman while he stood near the on-deck circle.
Bregman immediately left the game with blood visible on his face. He later underwent hospital testing after the ball struck him near his cheekbone.
The selfie, which he shared on his Instagram, showed significant swelling around Bregman's eye, along with facial cuts and a nosebleed. Especially the area below his eye had turned slightly black. He also included a message for supporters: "Thanks for all the messages, y'all. I'll be back 🙏."
Cubs manager Craig Counsell described the incident as a "terrible, terrible accident." He said the team's priority was getting positive medical results after Bregman was taken to the hospital.
The injury came during an important stretch for Chicago. The Cubs entered Sunday chasing a postseason berth and remained positioned for a National League wild-card spot.
Cubs must manage Alex Bregman's absence carefully

Bregman had already contributed during Sunday's game before leaving. He delivered an RBI single in the first inning, helping Chicago build an early lead.
After Bregman exited, Matt Shaw replaced him as a pinch-hitter. Pedro Ramirez shifted to third base while Shaw moved to second.
The Cubs continued producing offensively without their veteran third baseman. Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run, while Michael Conforto and Seiya Suzuki also homered.
Chicago now faces a balance between its postseason push and Bregman's recovery. His defensive stability and veteran experience remain valuable during the final week.
Counsell said Bregman's general well-being came before baseball considerations. "I want to get a good report first," the manager said.
Bregman's message offered some optimism, but his return timeline remains unclear. The Cubs will need to await further medical updates before determining his availability.

After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

CINCINNATI – Al comenzar el domingo el último juego de la serie contra los Rojos, el jardinero central de los Cachorros, Pete Crow-Armstrong, venía de un fin de semana frustrante, al irse de 10-0 con cuatro ponches en los primeros dos encuentros de la serie. Pero dejó atrás esos días complicados al quedarse a un triple de completar el ciclo y ayudar a Chicago a aplastar 9-1 a los Rojos en el Great American Ball Park.
La victoria dejó a los Cachorros un poco más cerca de la postemporada, pero necesitan que los Yankees derroten a los D-backs más tarde la tarde del domingo para asegurar oficialmente su boleto a octubre. Chicago tiene a su favor el criterio de desempate por enfrentamientos directos ante los Padres (5-1) y los Filis (6-1), los dos equipos que están por debajo en la lucha por los Comodines de la Liga Nacional, lo que le da ventaja en la pelea por obtener la localía para la Serie del Comodín, que comienza el 29 de septiembre.
Crow-Armstrong se fue de 5-3 con un jonrón y dos carreras impulsadas. Todo comenzó en el primer inning ante el derecho de los Rojos, Rhett Lowder. Crow-Armstrong conectó un sencillo al jardín derecho y luego se robó la segunda base, quedando a dos estafadas de lograr la primera temporada 40-40 en la historia de los Cachorros. Finalmente anotó con un sencillo de Alex Bregman, quien salió del juego en el cuarto episodio tras recibir en la cabeza el impacto de una pelota de foul conectada por su compañero Michael Busch.
Chicago anotó cuatro carreras ante Lowder en el tercer episodio, con PCA como principal protagonista. Abrió el inning con un doble y anotó la segunda rayita del juego gracias a un sencillo de Ian Happ. Fue el 30mo doble de la temporada para PCA, convirtiéndose en el 10mo jugador en la historia de Grandes Ligas con al menos una campaña de 40 o más jonrones, 30 o más dobles y 30 o más bases robadas, uniéndose al venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr., Jeff Bagwell (dos veces), Ryan Braun, Ellis Burks, el cubano José Canseco, Shohei Ohtani, Alex Rodríguez, el dominicano Alfonso Soriano y Larry Walker.
Crow-Armstrong luego conectó un cuadrangular en el quinto capítulo, su 45to de la temporada, para igualar a Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de MLB.
La estrella de los Cachorros tuvo una última oportunidad de conseguir el triple que le faltaba para completar el ciclo en el octavo acto ante Carson Spiers, pero elevó al campocorto dominicano Elly De La Cruz para el primer out de la entrada.

item.content:encoded:
After going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts in the first two games of this series, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had himself another big day in the third contest. PCA singled, doubled, homered and stole a base and helped lead the Cubs to a 9-1 blowout of the Reds, a victory tempered by a freak injury to Alex Bregman. More on the latter anon, first let’s wrap this win.
The Cubs got on the board in the first inning. PCA led off the game with a single and stole second, his 38th [VIDEO].
The Cubs extended their lead in the third. PCA led off with a double. A note on that double from BCB’s JohnW53:
With his third-inning double, Pete Crow-Armstrong has at least 30 homers, doubles and steals.
Only one Cub had done that before: PCA, last year.
Forty players on other teams have done it, 12 of them also multiple times. PCA is among 10 with two. Alfonso Soriano did it four times; Barry Bonds and Jose Ramirez, three.
It was noted on the Marquee broadcast that PCA’s 40-HR, 30-double, 30-steal year is the first ever by a MLB center fielder — nope, not Willie Mays, not Ken Griffey Jr., no one, until now. I’ve said it before, but don’t ever forget what you are seeing from Pete this year — it is truly historic.
Anyway, PCA then went to third on a ground out by Seiya Suzuki. The Cubs then loaded the bases on walks drawn by Michael Busch and Bregman.
Per the Marquee broadcast, that’s 22 bases-loaded walks for the Cubs this year, the most in MLB.
With the bases still loaded, Michael Conforto struck out, but Pedro Ramirez followed with a two-run single to make it 5-0 [VIDEO].
Now to the Bregman incident in the fourth inning. With two out, Busch hit a foul ball that struck Bregman, who was in the on-deck circle, in the face. Bregman immediately left the game and was replaced by Matt Shaw. Here’s what that looked like [VIDEO].
Per Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks, the ball hit Bregman in the cheekbone, which is swollen. There was also a facial cut, but we don’t know anything beyond that. Hopefully it’s not too serious and Bregman doesn’t have a concussion.
While all this was going on, David Peterson was sailing along, striking out seven over the first four innings. The Reds made it 5-1 on a solo homer by JJ Bleday in the fourth.
The Cubs got that run right back in the fifth on a solo homer by Michael Conforto, his 15th [VIDEO].
If you’re keeping track:
Kyle Tucker, 16 HR, 515 AB
Michael Conforto, 15 HR, 294 AB
That blast tied PCA with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. The Cubs also lead MLB in home runs with 217; as noted on the Marquee broadcast, the last time the Cubs led all of baseball in home runs was 1958, led by Ernie Banks with 47 in his first MVP season.
Peterson completed six innings, allowing three hits and just the one run on Bleday’s homer. Here are his seven strikeouts [VIDEO].
More on Peterson’s afternoon from BCB’s JohnW53:
David Peterson’s quality start was his fifth as a Cub, fourth most on the team. Shota Imanaga has 14, as many as the next two combined: Matthew Boyd, eight, and Colin Rea, six. Edward Cabrera and Jameson Taillon both have four. Five others have one to three.
Peterson could be a valuable weapon in the postseason, either as a starter or out of the bullpen.
The Cubs weren’t done homering, either. After Caleb Thielbar threw a scoreless seventh, Suzuki lofted his 25th into the batter’s eye to make it 9-1 [VIDEO].
More on recent Cubs home runs from John:
With their three home runs, the Cubs have hit nine in their last four games (three, one, two, three). They had hit 12 in their previous 14 games, since smacking a team-record nine at home vs. the Brewers on Aug. 31.
Edward Cabrera was given the eighth inning, a good low-leverage situation. He allowed a leadoff single and after retiring the next hitter, another Reds batter reached on an error by Ramirez. But Cabrera got Elly De La Cruz to hit into an inning-ending double play.
Colin Rea finished up with a 1-2-3 ninth, his first game action in 11 days, on just eight pitches. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
The Cubs will clinch a postseason berth if the Yankees defeat the Diamondbacks Sunday, a game that’s just begun at the time of this recap. The Padres, tied with the Cubs for the top wild card spot with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker, are playing the Marlins in a contest in San Diego that’s also just underway. The Phillies defeated the Mets Sunday, so the Cubs still lead Philadelphia by a game. Thanks to the Mets for taking two of the four games from the Phillies over the weekend.
The Cubs have Monday off, then open the final regular season home series Tuesday evening against the Marlins at Wrigley Field. Kevin Gausman will start for the Cubs and Janson Junk will go for Miami. Game time Tuesday is 6:40 p.m. CT and TV coverage will be via Marquee Sports Network.

CINCINNATI – Entering Sunday’s finale against the Reds, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had a frustrating weekend, going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts over the first two games of the series. But he made up for those difficult days by coming a triple shy of the cycle and helping Chicago pound the Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park.
The victory helped bring the Cubs an inch closer to the postseason, but they need the Yankees to beat the D-backs later Sunday afternoon to officially clinch October baseball. Chicago owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Padres (5-1) and the Phillies (6-1), the two teams below them in the NL Wild Card race, giving them the upper hand to earn home-field advantage for the Wild Card Series starting Sept. 29.
Crow-Armstrong went 3-for-5 with a homer and two RBIs. It all started in the first inning against Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder. Crow-Armstrong singled to right field and then stole second base, putting him two steals shy of the first 40-40 season in Cubs franchise history. He eventually scored on a single by Alex Bregman, who left the game in the fourth after getting hit in the head by a foul ball from teammate Michael Busch.
Chicago scored four runs off Lowder in the third frame, and it was PCA who led the charge. He led off with a double and scored the second run of the game on a single by Ian Happ. It was PCA’s 30th double of the season, making him the 10th player in Major League Baseball history to notch 40-plus homers, 30-plus doubles and 30-plus stolen bases in a season at least once, joining Ronald Acuña Jr., Jeff Bagwell (twice), Ryan Braun, Ellis Burks, Jose Canseco, Shohei Ohtani, Alex Rodriguez, Alfonso Soriano and Larry Walker.
Crow-Armstrong later homered in the fifth for his 45th blast of the season, tying him with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead.
The Cubs star got one last chance to tally the triple that would complete his cycle in the eighth against Carson Spiers, but he popped up to shortstop Elly De La Cruz for the first out of the inning.

item.content:encoded:
What a wild week in Chicago this was.
“You’re shaking your head in amazement sometimes,” Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell said earlier this week. “You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field.”
Counsell was referring to Pete Crow-Armstrong’s prolific night Wednesday against the Atlanta Braves, where the center fielder continued to build his case as unanimous National League MVP with two home runs and a triple.
Counsell could’ve used the same basic quote Friday night in Cincinnati when Michael Busch was thrown out at second to end a 6-4 loss to the Reds, leaving the Cubs in a three-way wild-card tie with the Philadelphia Phillies and San Diego Padres. Cubs fans watching on Marquee were shaking their heads in amazement because you don’t often see that happen on a baseball field either.
With the tying run at the plate in Ian Happ, there was no reason for Busch to try to take second, making the attempt a foolish risk.
“It was stupid,” Counsell told reporters afterward. “l’ll take responsibility for it. It was a dumb play.”
Confirmed.
It was good Counsell took the blame away from his player, since a simple “Stay put” order by the manager would’ve at least given Happ a chance for some ninth-inning heroics.
No, it wasn’t why the Cubs lost the game.
Starter Clay Holmes walked five and allowed six runs in 5 1/3 innings in a subpar outing, Javier Assad struggled in relief and Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-5 and stranded nine runners. No one is perfect, not even the face of the franchise.
But in a tight wild-card race in which every game matters, the Busch gaffe was the one that will be remembered if the Cubs don’t get home-field advantage in the wild-card round and are eliminated on the road. There’s still time to finish strong, and the Cubs are capable of winning a wild-card series away from Wrigley Field either way.
But unforced mistakes like that can’t happen at this time of year, as Counsell knows.
Meanwhile, White Sox manager Will Venable watched his usually reliable bullpen implode Friday night on the South Side, blowing a six-run lead in an 11-8 loss to the Detroit Tigers.
Sox fans roundly booed Venable during pitching moves, a rarity this season. Though Venable deserves credit for the Sox being in the race, his pitching decisions have come under fire of late, and the bullpen arms suddenly looked tired. But on Saturday he pushed all the right buttons in a 3-1 win over the Tigers, with Noah Schultz and Grant Taylor saving the win for Sean Burke.
Counsell and Venable are under pressure to get their teams into the playoffs, like every other manager with a contending team. Venable is playing with house money since nothing was expected of the Sox this season, but he’ll still get some of the blame if the team collapses after 2½ months in first place.
Counsell’s Cubs are a virtual shoo-in for a wild-card berth, but he’s also expected to take the Cubs deep into the postseason with one of the game’s elite players in Crow-Armstrong, a strong lineup and the best defense most of us have ever seen in Chicago.
Both managers have had good years overall, but it’s how they finish that eventually will define their seasons.
In a season as crazy as this, you knew it would come down to the final days.
No one said it was going to be easy. It never is when you’re a baseball fan in Chicago.
Clicks for coaches
Kudos to Blackhawks coach Jeff Blashill for reportedly refusing to let the Hawks media department film his opening speech to his players at the first full practice of training camp. This seems to be a common theme in sports these days — teams’ marketing departments trying to make the coach or manager into some kind of Knute Rockne figure for social media clicks.
Whatever Blashill said deserves to be private with his players, not the rest of the world. And as much as we enjoy Ben Johnson’s postgame speeches after wins, it wouldn’t be a bad idea for the Bears to keep it private once in a while.
Is the speech meant for the players or for the glorification of the coach? I’ll sit down and wait for my answer.
Swing-and-a-miss time
Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery is nearing the all-time single-season record of 223 strikeouts, set by the Arizona Diamondbacks’ Mark Reynolds in 2009. Montgomery entered Saturday tied for 10th with 213 strikeouts, one behind the current leader, the Philadelphia Phillies Kyle Schwarber, and had three more Saturday to make it 216.
Former Sox slugger Adam Dunn was one strikeout away from tying Reynolds’ record in 2012, but manager Robin Ventura sat him the final game, an act of mercy for the likeable Sox star in a meaningless game.
Venable needs Montgomery’s bat in the lineup in a tight playoff race, so he can’t afford to sit him to avoid setting the record. It’s up to Montgomery to avoid a date with the record book.
Birds of a feather
Hundreds of Ole Miss students chanted “A–hole” during LSU coach Lane Kiffin’s interview segment on Saturday’s “College GameDay.” Last week hundreds of Texas students relentlessly booed Texas Sen. Ted Cruz during the same show.
Which one deserved it more? It’s a toss-up.
Last call
Tigers pitcher Justin Verlander is retiring next week, making Sunday his final day at Rate Field as a player. Hopefully the Sox will give him a tribute, as other teams have done, since he was part of some great Tigers-Sox games on the South Side in his Hall of Fame career.
Medinah’s star turn
I’ve never been invited to be a member at Medinah Country Club, but if I were I’d ask the club to revoke the invitation to President Trump to be honorary chairman at this week’s Presidents Cup, just as he denied access to the White House for reporters of CNN, MS Now and Politico.
The invite was made by PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, who said in a statement Trump’s “participation will help elevate the event on the international stage while furthering our mission of bringing people together through the game of golf.”
They couldn’t have made a worse choice.

item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

Nolan Arenado, Diamondbacks (+630, DraftKings)
An important series in the desert opens tonight, and I'm sure there will be sellouts all weekend as the New York Yankees make a rare visit to Phoenix with a 9:40 ET first pitch. There are no weather concerns as Chase Field has a usually-closed retractable roof. It's not out of the question this could be a World Series preview. New York will be in the AL playoffs, most likely as the AL's top wild card team. Arizona has work to do to earn the NL's last wild card spot over San Diego.
And we get a Hall-of-Fame-caliber matchup in the bottom of the first in Yankees right-hander Gerrit Cole facing Diamondbacks third baseman Nolan Arenado. The one reason Cole might not get to Cooperstown is because his career is cut a bit short after injuries cost the 2023 Cy Young winner a chunk of the 2024 season and all of 2025. The 36-year-old righty has been moderately back in form this year at 8-9 with a 3.67 ERA. but has also allowed 20 homers in 20 starts.
Perhaps Cole is tiring as he has been ravaged for seven homers in back-to-back losses, allowing nine runs and 15 hits over 11 1/3 innings. In his most recent start against the Mets, Cole managed only three swings and misses, none generated by Cole's 38 fastballs.
There is no doubt Arenado will be headed to Cooperstown as arguably a top-10 third baseman in MLB history as a 10-time All-Star, eight-time Gold Glover, five-time Silver Slugger Award winner and three-time NL home run leader. The 35-year-old has one year left on that eight-year, $260 million contract originally signed with the Rockies in 2019. Arenado's 26 homers this season, his first with Arizona, are his most since 26 in 2023 with the Cardinals. He has hit 15 of those 26 at home and is 10-for-22 in his career off Cole with three homers and two doubles, good for a slugging percentage of .955.
Perhaps also consider a longshot flier on Snakes catcher James McCann, even though he only has five homers and doesn't play all the time. McCann is 6-for-14 with three doubles and a homer career off Cole.

These clubs are division leaders in very different senses. The Braves will win the NL East, while the Astros are neck-and-neck with the Rangers in the AL West and could miss the postseason entirely.
The Braves already did the Astros a solid for this series by opting to skip ace Chris Sale in it. That somewhat hints to me what Atlanta's motivation is the rest of the way as it apparently will not push overly hard to try and earn the NL's No. 2 seed and that first-round bye.

CINCINNATI -- Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman has been one of the best hitters in baseball in the second half of the 2026 season, and his hot streak extended from the field to the track. Bregman's horse won a race at Churchill Downs Thursday night, giving him and the Cubs reason to celebrate on a day off. Bregman had his entire team with him on a bus trip. The timing was perfect with the off day lining up just before a three-game series in Cincinnati, roughly a 90-minute drive from Louisville, home of Churchill Downs.
"It helps build the camaraderie, and it's fun," Bregman said. "I just think it's good to get the whole group together and having fun. That's what it's all about. Building that team chemistry, and it was a great time.
"That was probably a core memory for me right there. We've won probably 25 or 30 races, but that was the most meaningful. In terms of the size of the race, that was probably the smallest one we've ever won, but it was probably the most memorable because of all the guys being there."
Bregman's horse, Act of Parliament, was a winner with jockey Axel Concepcion. The Cubs' instagram account shared an 11-slide update of all the fun, which included second-year reliever Ryan Rolison dressed up in a horse costume, which he estimated felt like 100 degrees.
"Everyone was just going crazy watching the videos," said Rolison, who noted he would reuse the costume for Halloween. "We put the jockey up on our shoulders and I think he enjoyed that. Pedro [Ramírez] was walking me around by my ear. That was quite the experience. It was a great time. It was awesome."
Bregman isn't alone in his love for the horse track, as Cubs manager Craig Counsell also loved it.
"We just had a fun day, that's the big thing," Counsell said "Churchill Downs is a historic place, like Wrigley Field. It's like a Wrigley Field for horse racing. It was fun to introduce a bunch of guys on the team to a different world that they don't get to see and we got to hang out outside of baseball."
"It was cool to see, Breggy and Counsell love their horse races," said utility man Matt Shaw. "And for us to see and experience that. The horses were beautiful, the place was beautiful, it was really cool."
As noted, Bregman's hot streak is happening on and off the field.
Heading into Friday, Bregman in the second half of the season is hitting .305/.384/.623 with 17 homers and 47 RBI. He trails only his teammate and NL MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong in second-half WAR in all of baseball. He's second in slugging (again, to PCA), fourth in home runs and second (again, to PCA) in RBI.
All this came after a very disappointing first half, but Bregman puts in the work.
"He's just a relentless competitor," Counsell said. "We throw around the term 'baseball junkie' but that's just what he is. I joked the other day that he doesn't sleep, but I don't know if he sleeps. He's always looking for ways to get an advantage. It's more hours of the day than I have. That's just who he is. He's great at it. He loves doing it and it's fun to see."
The Cubs, who entered the weekend in possession of the National League's top wild-card spot with nine games remaining, hope to add a lot more fun and core memories in the 2026 postseason.

¿Quién es el mejor campocorto en el béisbol?
La respuesta convencional en este momento probablemente sería el torpedero de los Reales, Bobby Witt Jr., y con buen motivo. El joven de 26 años es un tres veces convocado al Juego de Estrellas y ganador de dos Guantes de Oro, dos Bates de Plata, un título de bateo en el 2023 y un Guante de Platino la temporada pasada. También ha terminado segundo y cuarto en la votación para Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana en cada una de las últimas dos campañas.
Sin embargo, ¿si le haces esa pregunta a la leyenda de los Rojos, Joey Votto? Recibirás una respuesta diferente. El JMV de la Liga Nacional del 2010 se unió a MLB Now el viernes y argumentó que Elly de la Cruz de Cincinnati es el mejor paracorto del béisbol.
Al entrar al juego del viernes, el dominicano tenía bateaba .284/.362/.517 con 29 dobles, 28 jonrones, 74 impulsadas, 150 hits, 26 bases robadas y OPS+ de 142 en 134 partidos. En comparación, Bobby Witt Jr. llevaba .276/.359/.441 con 30 dobles, 18 cuadrangulares, 54 empujadas, 144 imparables, 42 bases robadas y OPS+ de 126 en la misma cantidad de encuentros (134).
Votto argumentó que el estadio local de Witt (el Kauffman Stadium) favorece más su estilo de juego que el estadio local de De la Cruz (el Great American Ball Park). Ofensivamente, los números lo demuestran, ya que Witt batea .306/.376/.519 en casa esta temporada. En la ruta, sus números no son tan fuertes, ya que registra .245/.340/.360 en los juegos fuera de casa esta campaña.
Por otro lado, De la Cruz tiene .301/.395/.544 como local esta temporada y su ofensiva no ha disminuido tanto en la carretera. En sus partidos como visitante, batea .268/.329/.491.
El área en que Witt se destaca por encima de De la Cruz es la defensa. Witt es tercero en general en Grandes Ligas con 22 Outs Por Encima Del Promedio, cuarto en general en Valor De Carreras A La Defensa (16) y tiene ocho Carreras Defensivas Salvadas (DRS), según FanGraphs. De la Cruz tiene números mixtos en esas métricas, ya que tiene ocho Outs Por Encima Del Promedio (empatado en el puesto 33), cinco en Valor De Carreras A La Defensa (empatado en el puesto 62) y -6 Carreras Defensivas Salvadas.
Votto argumentó que la defensa es lo único que impide que De la Cruz sea uno de los mejores jugadores de las Mayores.
"Probablemente ésa sea la última pieza del rompecabezas [para ponerlo] en la categoría de [Shohei] Ohtani, ponerlo en ésa de [Aaron] Judge, ponerlo en ésa de 'mejor jugador del deporte' -- Pete Crow-Armstrong --", expresó Votto.
